title: From FASTQ to Nextflow
text:
0.1 What you will build
You can understand modern bioinformatics workflow engineering without already being a programmer. This book starts with ordinary sequencing files and shell commands, then develops one small analysis into a reproducible Nextflow workflow that can run locally or through an HPC scheduler.
By the end, you will have followed the reasoning behind:

title: From FASTQ to Nextflow
From FASTQ to Nextflow
text:
0.2 Who this book is for
This book is written for biologists who can use a web browser but may not yet know what a shell, software channel, container image, workflow channel or job scheduler is. Every new term is introduced before it is relied upon.






ImportantScientific scope



The example uses deterministic synthetic paired-end reads derived from human GRCh38 chromosome 22. It contains no patient data. It is a teaching and reproducibility artifact—not a clinical pipeline, a WGBS pipeline or a production-scale biological analysis.

title: From FASTQ to Nextflow
Preface
text:
Companion project
This tutorial grew from a real workflow-portability exercise on the DLDCC HPC cluster at Baylor College of Medicine. The useful parts were not only the successful commands. The difficult parts—an incompatible Java garbage collector, a full home-directory quota, a broken package solve, container PATH differences and non-identical BAM headers—exposed the engineering ideas that a beginner most needs to understand.
The book therefore preserves failures as teaching material. An error message is not evidence that you are unsuited to computational work. It is an observation about a system. The goal is to learn how to turn that observation into a small, testable hypothesis.
The commands and evidence are grounded in version v0.1.0 of the NGS Workflow Portability Lab. Linking the book to a tagged release prevents the underlying example from silently changing while someone is following the tutorial.

title: Preface
text:
A note about HPC systems
Cluster names, module names, partitions, accounts and storage paths are local policy. DLDCC-specific commands are labeled as examples. Readers should ask their own administrators for the equivalent settings rather than copying site configuration blindly.

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.1 Why a biologist should care
Imagine that you receive paired-end sequencing reads and answer a biological question with four programs. You record the commands in a notebook. Six months later, one program has changed, a library is missing and the commands run in the wrong order on a new computer. A collaborator cannot reproduce the result. On an HPC cluster, the same commands compete for memory or accidentally run on the login node.
The biological logic may have been correct. The engineering around it was not strong enough to preserve and communicate that logic.
Modern bioinformatics therefore has two inseparable responsibilities:
This book concentrates on the second responsibility without pretending it can replace the first. A beautifully engineered workflow can still run an inappropriate aligner. A biologically appropriate analysis can still be unreproducible if its software and execution are undocumented. Industry teams need both kinds of judgment.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
Analytical responsibility: choose methods that are appropriate for the biological question and interpret their outputs correctly.
Engineering responsibility: make the inputs, software, execution, decisions and outputs traceable, testable and repeatable.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.2 Engineering objective
Before installing or coding anything, we need a map of the system. You should be able to point to each layer and answer:

What problem does this layer solve?
What information enters and leaves it?
Which other layer does it depend on?
What evidence tells us that it behaved as intended?

If these layers are blurred together, troubleshooting becomes guesswork. For example, changing a Conda package cannot fix a SLURM account error, and changing a Nextflow channel cannot repair a corrupt FASTQ file.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.3 Start with files and transformations
Most command-line bioinformatics programs behave like transformations:
input files + parameters + software → output files + logs
In our teaching project:

FastQC reads FASTQ files and writes quality reports.
Trim Galore reads paired FASTQ files and writes trimmed paired FASTQ files plus reports.
Bowtie2 reads trimmed FASTQ files and a reference index, then writes SAM alignment records.
SAMtools sorts, indexes and validates the alignments in BAM format.

Each program is a tool. A tool normally performs one focused operation. Connecting the tools creates a pipeline.





flowchart LR
    R["Paired FASTQ"] --> Q1["Raw FastQC"]
    R --> T["Trim Galore"]
    T --> Q2["Post-trim FastQC"]
    T --> A["Bowtie2"]
    X["Reference index"] --> A
    A --> S["SAMtools sort"]
    S --> V["BAM validation"]


 The analytical path used throughout the book. Trimming creates two branches: post-trim quality control and alignment. 



Notice that this is not simply a list. Raw FastQC and trimming can begin from the same input. Post-trim FastQC and alignment must wait for trimming. Alignment also needs the reference index. These dependencies form a directed graph.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
section: 2.4 Tool, command, script, pipeline and workflow
text:
2.4 Tool, command, script, pipeline and workflow
These words are related but not interchangeable.








Term
Meaning in this book
Example




Tool
A program that performs a focused operation
samtools


Command
One request to run a program with particular arguments
samtools quickcheck sample.bam


Script
A saved text file containing commands and control logic
run_manual.sh


Pipeline
The connected analytical steps from input to result
FASTQ → trim → align → BAM


Workflow
An executable model of tasks, dependencies, inputs, outputs and resources
main.nf


Workflow run
One execution of a workflow with specific inputs, settings and software
the five-task chr22 run



A Bash script can implement a pipeline. A workflow engine adds explicit task contracts, dependency scheduling, isolated work directories, caching, resource requests and alternative execution backends. That does not make Bash obsolete: every Nextflow process in this book ultimately runs shell commands.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.5 The complete stack
Our analytical graph sits inside a larger engineering system.





flowchart TB
    BQ["Biological question"] --> DATA["Input data + metadata"]
    DATA --> WF["Nextflow workflow logic"]
    SW["Software layer<br/>Conda environment or OCI image"] --> WF
    CFG["Parameters + configuration"] --> WF
    WF --> EX["Executor<br/>local or SLURM"]
    EX --> RT["Task runtime<br/>host, Conda or Singularity"]
    RT --> OUT["Outputs + logs + reports"]
    OUT --> QC["Technical and biological review"]
    GIT["Git + GitHub<br/>history and collaboration"] -. records .-> WF
    GIT -. records .-> CFG
    CI["CI/CD automation"] -. checks and publishes .-> GIT


 The layers are complementary. Nextflow coordinates commands supplied by an environment or image and launches tasks through an executor. 



The arrows do not mean that Git executes FastQC or that SLURM installs SAMtools. Each layer has a narrower responsibility.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.6 The host operating system
The host is the computer or compute node on which a process ultimately runs. It supplies the kernel, processors, memory, filesystems and security controls. On a laptop you may administer much of the host. On an institutional cluster, platform administrators control it.
This matters because neither Conda nor a container creates CPUs or memory. Containers also share the host kernel; they are not complete virtual machines. Architecture and operating-system compatibility still matter.
Question answered by the host: What machine resources and operating-system services exist?
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.7 Cluster modules
An HPC module system lets administrators offer multiple versions of cluster-provided software. Loading a module commonly modifies environment variables such as PATH, which controls where the shell searches for executables.
Examples might include Java, Singularity or a compiler. Module names and versions are local to the cluster.
Question answered by modules: Which administrator-provided software should this shell session see?
Modules are not Conda environments. A module may expose the Java needed to start Nextflow while a Conda environment supplies FastQC and SAMtools. Because both can modify PATH, they can also conflict. Later we will inspect the active layers rather than assuming which executable is being used.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.8 Conda environments and channels
Conda is a package and environment manager. A Conda environment is an isolated directory containing selected programs and their dependencies. For example, SAMtools depends on libraries for compressed genomic file formats. Conda attempts to choose a compatible set.
A channel is a package repository. It is a source from which Conda obtains package metadata and package files. Bioconda distributes many bioinformatics packages; conda-forge distributes a broad range of supporting software and libraries. Channel order and priority affect which builds the solver may select.
Question answered by Conda: Which package versions and compatible libraries are installed in this environment?
Conda improves control over software, but an environment specification alone does not freeze the host kernel, scheduler, external reference data or every future package build. Reproducibility has multiple layers.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.9 OCI images, Docker and containers
An OCI image is a packaged, read-only filesystem plus metadata describing how software should run. OCI refers to open container standards. Docker is one widely used platform for building and running OCI-compatible images.
A container is a running process created from an image. The distinction is similar to a class recipe versus one instantiated object, or a cake recipe versus one baked cake—although every analogy has limits.
An image can contain the Conda-resolved tools, their libraries and selected operating-system files. A registry such as GitHub Container Registry stores and distributes images.








Concept
Mutable while building/running?
Role




Dockerfile
Yes, it is source text
Recipe for building an image


Image
Normally treated as immutable
Packaged filesystem and metadata


Tag
Can be moved to another image
Human-friendly name such as v0.1.0


Digest
Identifies exact image content
Immutable content address


Container
Has a writable runtime layer
A process running from an image


Registry
Stores and distributes images
GHCR, Docker Hub or another service



Question answered by an image: What packaged userspace and tools should travel with this task?






WarningA tag is not an immutable identity



The label latest can point to different image content tomorrow. A digest identifies exact content. Friendly tags are useful for humans; digests are stronger evidence for an exact runtime.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.10 Singularity and Apptainer on HPC
Docker normally relies on a long-running privileged service called a daemon. Multi-user HPC centers commonly do not allow users to run that service. They often provide Singularity or Apptainer, which can execute container images using an HPC-oriented security and filesystem model.
Singularity can pull an OCI image and create a SIF—a Singularity Image Format file. Nextflow can then execute individual tasks inside that SIF while SLURM assigns the compute node.
Docker and Singularity therefore are not two words for the same operation in our project:

GitHub Actions uses a Docker-oriented build process to create the OCI image.
DLDCC uses Singularity to run the resulting image as a SIF.

Question answered by Singularity: How should this HPC task enter and run the packaged container environment?
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.12 Executors and SLURM
An executor is the Nextflow component that decides how tasks are launched. With the local executor, tasks run on the current machine. With the SLURM executor, Nextflow writes job wrappers and submits them to the cluster scheduler.
SLURM is a workload manager. It places jobs on shared compute resources according to requested CPUs, memory, time, partition, account and site policy. It tracks queued, running, completed and failed jobs.
SLURM does not understand that trimming must precede alignment. Nextflow knows the data dependency and submits the alignment task only when its inputs exist. Nextflow does not decide which physical node is free. SLURM does.
Question answered by the executor and scheduler: How, where and when should this ready task run?
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
section: 2.13 Git and GitHub: traceable change and collaboration
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.14 CI/CD: automated feedback and delivery
Continuous integration (CI) means automatically integrating and checking small changes frequently. A CI workflow may lint files, render documentation, run a small test and verify that a container contains required tools.
Continuous delivery means keeping a tested artifact ready to release or publishing it through a controlled process. Continuous deployment goes further: a passing change is automatically deployed to its target environment.
In our work:

GitHub Actions building and smoke-checking an image is CI plus artifact delivery.
GitHub Actions publishing this Quarto book to GitHub Pages is automated deployment of documentation.
Running a research pipeline on new samples is not automatically “CI/CD.” It is a workflow execution and may require separate authorization, review and data controls.

Automation supplies evidence; it does not create scientific truth. A green check means the configured checks passed—not that every biological or clinical requirement has been validated.
Question answered by CI/CD: Which checks and publication actions should happen automatically when source changes or a release is created?
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
section: 2.15 Trace one sample through the stack
text:
2.15 Trace one sample through the stack
Consider the sample identifier sim_chr22.

Two FASTQ files and sample metadata describe the input.
Git identifies the exact workflow, configuration, environment and container recipe revision.
Nextflow creates the raw-QC and trimming tasks because both can consume the original read pair.
The selected profile tells Nextflow to use the local or SLURM executor and a Conda environment or Singularity image.
On DLDCC, Nextflow submits a job wrapper to SLURM.
SLURM assigns a compute node with the requested resources.
Singularity starts the task inside the project SIF and makes required host paths visible through bind mounts.
FastQC or Trim Galore runs with the inputs staged by Nextflow.
The task writes output and logs in its isolated work directory.
Nextflow records task status, publishes selected results and enables cache reuse.
Technical checks confirm that files exist, are readable and have expected summaries.
A qualified analyst still decides whether the results are biologically meaningful for the intended use.

No single technology performs all twelve responsibilities.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.16 Three kinds of reproducibility
The word reproducible is often used too broadly. In this book we separate:

Computational repeatability: rerunning the same inputs, code, parameters and runtime produces acceptably equivalent outputs.
Computational reproducibility: another person can reconstruct the analysis from recorded source, software, data provenance and instructions.
Scientific reproducibility: independent evidence supports the same scientific conclusion.

This project primarily demonstrates the first two on a small synthetic test fixture. It does not demonstrate clinical validation or independent scientific replication.






ImportantEngineering evidence has a scope



A successful Nextflow run proves that configured tasks completed. A valid BAM proves that the file passes selected structural checks. A container digest identifies image content. None of these facts alone proves that a method is appropriate for diagnosis, that a biological conclusion is correct or that the workflow is production-ready.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.17 Common misconceptions

2.17.1 “Conda and Docker do the same thing”
Both help control software, but at different boundaries. Conda manages packages inside an environment. An OCI image packages a broader userspace and metadata. We will use Conda to resolve tools and then package that environment in an image.


2.17.2 “Nextflow runs the cluster”
Nextflow models and submits work. SLURM manages shared cluster resources. The Nextflow SLURM executor connects the two.


2.17.3 “The container includes my input data”
Our image contains software, not the large analysis inputs. At runtime, files are normally mounted or staged into the container.


2.17.4 “If CI is green, the pipeline is validated”
CI reports only the checks we encoded. Validation requires defined intended use, requirements, acceptance criteria, evidence and—where applicable—formal quality or regulatory processes.


2.17.5 “GitHub is Git”
Git is the version-control system. GitHub is a hosting and collaboration platform built around Git repositories. Git works without GitHub.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.19 Verification checkpoint
Match each scenario to its primary layer. Some scenarios involve several layers; choose the one that owns the stated decision.

SAMtools 1.19.2 and its libraries must be installed together.
Trimming must finish before alignment begins.
Five ready tasks are waiting for available compute nodes.
An HPC task must enter the project SIF before running FastQC.
A reviewer wants to inspect the exact source change that introduced a new parameter.
A pushed pull request should automatically render the documentation and run a smoke test.
A collaborator wants the exact image content rather than whatever latest means today.
An analyst must decide whether Bowtie2 is appropriate for bisulfite-treated reads.







TipShow the answers






Conda/package environment.
Nextflow workflow dependency.
SLURM scheduler.
Singularity/Apptainer runtime.
Git history and GitHub review.
CI automation.
OCI image digest.
Biological/methodological judgment—not the workflow engine.




You are ready to continue when you can explain why each answer is different, not merely recite the product names.

title: 2  The whole shebang
text:
2.21 What to remember

Biological validity and engineering reproducibility support one another but are not the same claim.
A tool performs an operation; a workflow engine coordinates operations and their dependencies.
Modules, Conda, containers, Nextflow and SLURM solve different problems and can be used together.
Docker/OCI builds and distributes the image; Singularity/Apptainer executes that packaged environment on our HPC system.
Git records source history; GitHub supports collaboration; CI/CD automates explicitly defined checks and delivery.
Every green check, checksum and report has a limited meaning. Good engineers state that meaning accurately.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 3  The terminal and an HPC cluster
text:
This chapter introduces prompts, commands, login versus compute nodes, software modules, storage locations and job schedulers. It explains why heavy analyses should not be run on a shared login node and why module purge changes the cluster-provided software layer without deactivating a Conda environment.






NoteComing in the guided build



The complete lesson will use annotated DLDCC examples while clearly marking which paths, module names, accounts and partitions are site-specific.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model
3  The terminal and an HPC cluster

title: 4  Files, paths and Git
text: This chapter develops the minimum command-line vocabulary needed for the rest of the book: working directories, absolute and relative paths, files versus directories, standard output, exit codes, checksums, Git commits and tags.
crumbs: Part I — Build the mental model

title: 5  Conda environments
text: This chapter explains packages, dependencies, environments, channels, channel priority and version pinning. It then builds the tool environment and uses version commands to prove which executables are active.
crumbs: Part II — Build a trusted manual workflow

title: 6  A deterministic test fixture
text: This chapter downloads GRCh38 chromosome 22, generates deterministic synthetic paired reads and records SHA-256 checksums. It explains why small, non-sensitive test data are essential for rapid development and public reproducibility.
crumbs: Part II — Build a trusted manual workflow

title: 7  Establish a trusted manual pipeline
text: This chapter runs raw QC, paired trimming, post-trim QC, alignment, sorting, indexing and BAM validation one operation at a time. The manual result becomes the baseline against which automation is judged.
crumbs: Part II — Build a trusted manual workflow
7  Establish a trusted manual pipeline

title: 8  Turn commands into strict Bash
text: This chapter combines validated commands into a script and explains set -euo pipefail one option at a time. Checksums and biological summary statistics are used to confirm that automation preserved the baseline result.
crumbs: Part II — Build a trusted manual workflow
8  Turn commands into strict Bash

title: 9  Container mental model
text: This chapter distinguishes an image, a running container, a registry, an image tag and an immutable digest. It also explains what containers do—and do not—do for reproducibility.
crumbs: Part III — Make the software portable

title: 10  Build the project image
text: This chapter reads the Dockerfile from top to bottom, builds the OCI image with GitHub Actions and records evidence about its contents. Special attention is given to layers, executable paths and pinned packages.
crumbs: Part III — Make the software portable

title: 11  Run the image with Singularity
text: This chapter pulls the OCI image into a SIF file and runs tools with singularity exec --cleanenv. It uses the real PATH and ps failures to show how container-runtime assumptions can differ between Docker and HPC execution.
crumbs: Part III — Make the software portable
11  Run the image with Singularity

title: 12  Nextflow mental model
text: This chapter introduces processes, channels, values, paths, task working directories, dataflow and publishDir without yet constructing the complete workflow.
crumbs: Part IV — Port the workflow to Nextflow

title: 13  Your first Nextflow process
text: This chapter builds a minimal DSL2 workflow, examines .command.sh, .command.run, .command.log and .exitcode, then ports raw FastQC as the first real process.
crumbs: Part IV — Port the workflow to Nextflow

title: 14  Complete the DSL2 workflow
text: This chapter adds paired trimming, post-trim QC, alignment and BAM validation. Each input/output declaration is related back to the corresponding manual files so readers can see how a shell pipeline becomes a dataflow graph.
crumbs: Part IV — Port the workflow to Nextflow

title: 15  Profiles and software runtimes
text: This chapter defines Conda-local, Singularity-local and SLURM-Singularity profiles. It explains the separation between workflow logic, software runtime and execution platform.
crumbs: Part IV — Port the workflow to Nextflow

title: 16  Submit tasks through SLURM
text: This chapter examines the SLURM executor, resource requests and generated #SBATCH directives. It verifies that each of the five processes ran as a scheduled job inside the intended container.
crumbs: Part V — Execute and prove it

title: 17  Failure tests and resume caching
text: This chapter deliberately supplies a missing input pattern, checks the nonzero exit code and interprets the error. It then uses -resume and a trace file to prove that all five completed tasks were restored from cache.
crumbs: Part V — Execute and prove it
17  Failure tests and resume caching

title: 18  What reproducibility really means
text: This chapter compares Conda and container outputs. It explains why whole BAM hashes differed because provenance headers recorded different executable paths, while headerless alignment records, flagstat and idxstats remained identical.
crumbs: Part V — Execute and prove it

title: 19  Release an evidence-backed project
text: This chapter cleans the repository, creates a semantic version tag and connects each engineering claim to a reviewable artifact. It also teaches readers how to describe limitations without weakening the work.
crumbs: Part V — Execute and prove it

title: 20  Glossary
text:
Channel
A Nextflow dataflow object that carries values between workflow components.
Conda environment
An isolated collection of software packages and their dependencies.
Container image
An immutable package of files and metadata used to create a container runtime.
Executor
The Nextflow component that determines how tasks are launched, such as locally or through SLURM.
Process
A Nextflow definition describing a repeatable unit of work, its inputs, outputs and command script.
SLURM
A workload manager that schedules jobs and allocates shared cluster resources.

title: 21  Troubleshooting
text:
The final appendix will organize the real failures from the companion project by symptom, diagnostic observation, root cause, fix and durable lesson.
Initial cases include Java G1 initialization failure, home-directory quota exhaustion, Conda dependency solving, missing container PATH entries, missing ps, invalid SAMtools options and misleading whole-file BAM hashes.

title: 22  Command reference
text: This appendix will collect the small set of shell, Git, Conda, Singularity, Nextflow and SLURM commands introduced in the lessons. It is a memory aid, not a replacement for understanding the commands in context.

title: 23  Next steps
text: After completing the book, readers will be directed toward Nextflow training, nf-core conventions, larger test suites, workflow modules, continuous integration and domain-appropriate aligners. These are presented as future skills rather than accomplishments of the teaching pipeline.
